title: Iphis
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: In Crete a freeborn commoner of small means tells his pregnant wife that if she bears a daughter the child must be killed at birth. Isis appears to her in a dream and tells her to raise whatever is born; the girl is brought up as a boy and given a name that fits either sex. In Iphis' thirteenth year the father betroths her to Ianthe, the two love each other equally, and Iphis breaks out in a long speech against a love she says no female animal has ever felt — until, on the eve of the wedding, her mother prays at the goddess's altar.

sentences.t:
Fama novi centum Cretaeas forsitan urbes
implesset monstri, si non miracula nuper
Iphide mutata Crete propiora tulisset.
sentences.l: The report of the new portent would perhaps have filled the hundred Cretan cities, if Crete had not lately borne marvels nearer home, with Iphis changed.
sentences.i: Word of that new portent might have filled the hundred cities of Crete, had Crete not lately produced a marvel closer to home — the changing of Iphis.
sentences.n: A past unreal condition: implesset (a shortened implevisset) and tulisset are both pluperfect subjunctive, so the filling never happened. Iphide mutata is an ablative absolute — a self-contained “with Iphis changed” where English wants a clause; the construction runs through this part, and the participle mutata is feminine, agreeing with Iphis. The portent whose fame is in question, monstri, is not Iphis' own change: that is the miracula propiora, the nearer marvels which — the condition says — kept the report from spreading. The noun itself returns as monstra in Iphis' own mouth at IX.736.

sentences.t:
Proxima Cnosiaco nam quondam Phaestia regno
progenuit tellus ignotum nomine Ligdum,
ingenua de plebe virum.
sentences.l: For the land of Phaestus, nearest to the Cnossian kingdom, once brought forth Ligdus, unknown in name, a man of freeborn common stock.
sentences.i: For the country of Phaestus, next to the kingdom of Cnossos, once produced Ligdus — a man nobody had heard of, freeborn but common.
sentences.n: Phaestia tellus and Cnosiaco regno are two Cretan places set side by side, and Dicte follows at IX.717; Phaestus supplies the women called Phaestiadas at IX.716. Ignotum nomine is an ablative of respect, “unknown as to his name”. Ingenua de plebe marks him as freeborn but not noble.

sentences.t:
Nec census in illo
nobilitate sua maior, sed vita fidesque
inculpata fuit.
sentences.l: Nor was the property in him greater than his own rank, but his life and his good faith were blameless.
sentences.i: His means were no greater than his station, but his life and his word were beyond reproach.
sentences.n: Census is the assessed property that fixes a man's rank; the point is that he had no more money than his low birth implied. Inculpata is a single adjective serving both vita and fides, with a singular verb fuit beside them, so English has to double it or, as here, keep one word for both.

sentences.t:
Gravidae qui coniugis aures
vocibus his monuit, cum iam prope partus adesset:
sentences.l: And he warned the ears of his pregnant wife with these words, when now the birth was close at hand:
sentences.i: And this is what he said to his pregnant wife, when the birth was already close:
sentences.n: Qui is a connecting relative opening the sentence — “and he”, not “who”; the pattern recurs at IX.690. Aures monuit, “warned the ears”, is the Latin idiom for putting words into someone's hearing. Cum ... adesset is the circumstantial cum with imperfect subjunctive.

sentences.t:
“Quae voveam, duo sunt; minimo ut relevere dolore,
utque marem parias;
sentences.l: “The things I am to pray for are two: that you be relieved with the least pain, and that you bear a male;
sentences.i: “There are two things I have to pray for: that you get off with as little pain as possible, and that you bear a boy;
sentences.n: Quae voveam is a relative clause with the deliberative subjunctive — “the things I am to vow”, not “which I vow”. The two ut-clauses stand in apposition to duo and spell out the two prayers. Relevere is the alternative second-person singular ending for releveris, present passive subjunctive, so the literal keeps it passive: “that you be relieved”.

sentences.t:
onerosior altera sors est,
et vires fortuna negat.
sentences.l: the other lot is more burdensome, and fortune denies the strength.
sentences.i: the other outcome is the heavier burden, and fortune has not given us the means for it.
sentences.n: Sors is the lot that falls to you, here the sex of the child. Vires is “strength” in the sense of resources; what fortune withholds is the wherewithal to raise a daughter, and the man's poverty at IX.671–672 is what stands behind the word.

sentences.t:
Quod abominor, ergo
edita forte tuo fuerit si femina partu,
(invitus mando: pietas, ignosce!) necetur.”
sentences.l: And that I pray against — therefore, if by chance a female shall have been brought forth in your delivery (unwilling I give the order: dutifulness, forgive me!), let her be killed.”
sentences.i: And that is what I pray against — so, if it turns out a girl is delivered in your labour (I give the order unwillingly: dutifulness, forgive me!), let her be killed.”
sentences.n: Quod is again a connecting relative, picking up the outcome just named. Edita fuerit is future perfect passive, the ordinary tense in a Latin condition looking forward; necetur is a jussive present subjunctive, passive — “let her be killed”, with no agent named. Pietas, the duty owed to family and gods, is addressed as though it were a person standing by; he asks its pardon in the act of giving the order, and does not withdraw it.

sentences.t:
Dixerat, et lacrimis vultus lavere profusis,
tam qui mandabat, quam cui mandata dabantur.
sentences.l: He had spoken, and with tears poured out they washed their faces, both the one who was giving the orders and the one to whom the orders were being given.
sentences.i: He had spoken, and both of them bathed their faces in streaming tears — the one giving the orders and the one they were given to.
sentences.n: Lavere is lavērunt, the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere that this poem uses constantly; expect it wherever a perfect looks like an infinitive (accepere at IX.719, valuere at IX.756, tremuere at IX.783). Tam ... quam pairs the two weeping parties, one active and one passive: mandabat against mandata dabantur. Magnus prints vultus, faces in the plural for the two of them; some editions print the singular vultum.

sentences.t:
Sed tamen usque suum vanis Telethusa maritum
sollicitat precibus, ne spem sibi ponat in arto.
Certa sua est Ligdo sententia.
sentences.l: But all the same Telethusa keeps working on her own husband with prayers that get nowhere, that he not set her hope for her in a narrow place. Ligdus' verdict is fixed for him.
sentences.i: But Telethusa keeps at her husband all the same, with prayers that get nowhere, not to set her hope in so cramped a place. Ligdus' mind is made up.
sentences.n: Vanis, “empty”, judges the prayers before they are made: they fail. Ponat in arto is spatial — to set a thing in a cramped place — and the hope belongs to her, sibi. Certa sua est Ligdo sententia puts the dative of the person beside the possessive: the verdict is his own and it is settled.

sentences.t:
Iamque ferendo
vix erat illa gravem maturo pondere ventrem,
sentences.l: And by now she was scarcely equal to carrying a belly heavy with its ripe weight,
sentences.i: And by now she could barely carry the weight of a belly grown heavy and ready,
sentences.n: Ferendo is a dative gerund with erat, the Latin way of saying “was up to” a task. Maturo pondere is the ablative with gravem: heavy by reason of a weight now ripe, that is, at term.

sentences.t:
cum medio noctis spatio sub imagine somni
Inachis ante torum, pompa comitata sacrorum,
aut stetit aut visa est.
sentences.l: when in the middle span of the night, under the likeness of a dream, the daughter of Inachus, accompanied by a procession of her rites, either stood before the bed or seemed to.
sentences.i: when in the middle of the night, in the shape a dream takes, the daughter of Inachus stood before the bed, or seemed to, with a whole procession of her worship around her.
sentences.n: Inachis, “daughter of Inachus”, names the goddess by her father and by nothing else; the Latin gives her no other name until the mother addresses her as Isi at IX.773. Comitata is the perfect participle of the deponent comitor and is passive in force here, “accompanied by”, with the ablative pompa. Aut stetit aut visa est refuses to decide between vision and presence, and the poem does the same again at IX.782 with visa dea est.

sentences.t:
Inerant lunaria fronti
cornua cum spicis nitido flaventibus auro
et regale decus.
sentences.l: There were on her forehead moon-shaped horns, with ears of grain yellow with shining gold, and a royal splendour.
sentences.i: On her forehead were horns shaped like the moon, ears of grain yellow with bright gold, and a royal ornament.
sentences.n: Fronti is dative with inerant, “were in/on her forehead”. Lunaria cornua returns as imitata lunam cornua at IX.783–784, when the sign is given. Flaventibus auro is an ablative of cause: the gold is what makes the grain yellow.

sentences.t:
Cum qua latrator Anubis
sanctaque Bubastis variusque coloribus Apis,
quique premit vocem digitoque silentia suadet,
sentences.l: And with her were the barker Anubis and holy Bubastis and Apis, mottled with colours, and the one who presses down his voice and with his finger urges silence,
sentences.i: With her came Anubis the barker, holy Bubastis, Apis dappled in colours, and the one who holds his voice down and calls for silence with a finger,
sentences.n: Cum qua is a connecting relative — “and with her”. Latrator makes a noun of the barking, the one identifying mark Anubis is given here. The last figure is described and not named: the Latin supplies only the pressed-down voice and the finger that calls for silence, and no name is given for him anywhere in this part.

sentences.t:
sistraque erant numquamque satis quaesitus Osiris
plenaque somniferis serpens peregrina venenis.
sentences.l: and there were rattles, and Osiris never sought enough, and the foreign serpent full of sleep-bringing venoms.
sentences.i: and there were the rattles, and Osiris, never searched for enough, and the foreign snake, full of venom that brings sleep.
sentences.n: Erant governs the whole list, back through IX.690. Numquam satis quaesitus is a perfect passive participle with an adverb attached: the searching for Osiris is never finished. Somniferis venenis is an ablative with plena; venenum is any potent fluid, so “venom” here is what causes sleep rather than what kills. The sistrum named here is the instrument that sounds again at IX.784.

sentences.t:
Tum velut excussam somno et manifesta videntem
sic adfata dea est:
sentences.l: Then the goddess addressed her thus, as one shaken out of sleep and seeing plain things:
sentences.i: Then the goddess spoke to her like this, as though she were shaken awake and seeing it all clearly:
sentences.n: Excussam is an accusative feminine participle and videntem stands with it, both agreeing with an unexpressed object of adfata est, which has to be supplied from the situation — Telethusa. Adfata est is the deponent adfor and is active in sense: she addressed her. Velut hedges it, exactly as aut visa est did at IX.688.

sentences.t:
“Pars o Telethusa mearum,
pone graves curas mandataque falle mariti.
sentences.l: “O Telethusa, part of my own women, lay down your heavy cares and cheat your husband's orders.
sentences.i: “Telethusa, you who are one of mine, put down your heavy cares and get around your husband's orders.
sentences.n: Mearum is a feminine genitive plural with no noun: “of my women”, the goddess's own worshippers, supplied from the ending alone. Fallere is “to escape notice of, cheat”; the instruction is not to defy the order openly but to evade it, and that is what the rest of the tale does.

sentences.t:
Nec dubita, cum te partu Lucina levarit,
tollere quidquid erit.
sentences.l: And do not hesitate, when Lucina has relieved you of your delivery, to raise up whatever it will be.
sentences.i: And do not hesitate, once Lucina has brought you through the birth, to take up whatever it turns out to be.
sentences.n: Tollere is literally “lift up”, and it is set directly against the necetur of IX.679: the one order is to kill the newborn, the other to pick it up. Levarit is the shortened future perfect levaverit; te partu levare is “relieve you of your burden”, with the ablative of separation. Quidquid erit refuses to name a sex, which is the point.

sentences.t:
Dea sum auxiliaris opemque
exorata fero, nec te coluisse quereris
ingratum numen.” Monuit thalamoque recessit.
sentences.l: I am a goddess who helps, and entreated I bring aid, nor will you complain that you have worshipped an ungrateful divinity.” She gave her warning and withdrew from the chamber.
sentences.i: I am a goddess who helps: ask me and I bring aid, and you will not complain that the power you worshipped was thankless.” With that warning she withdrew from the room.
sentences.n: Exorata is a perfect passive participle, feminine, agreeing with the goddess: “having been prayed to”. Coluisse is a perfect infinitive in an accusative-and-infinitive after quereris, with te as its subject accusative; ingratum numen is its object. The verb monuit is the same one used of Ligdus' order at IX.674 — the two instructions, his and hers, are given the same word.

sentences.t:
Laeta toro surgit purasque ad sidera supplex
Cressa manus tollens, rata sint sua visa, precatur.
sentences.l: Glad, the Cretan woman rises from the bed and, a suppliant raising pure hands to the stars, prays that her visions be ratified.
sentences.i: The Cretan woman rises gladly from the bed and, lifting clean hands to the stars in supplication, prays that what she has seen may hold good.
sentences.n: Cressa, “the Cretan woman”, stands for Telethusa. Rata sint sua visa is an object clause of wishing with no ut, the subjunctive alone carrying the prayer. Manus tollens picks up the goddess's own tollere at IX.699, the same verb in a different sense.

sentences.t:
Ut dolor increvit, seque ipsum pondus in auras
expulit et nata est ignaro femina patre,
sentences.l: When the pain grew, and the weight itself drove itself out into the air, and a female was born with the father unaware,
sentences.i: When the pains came on, and the burden forced its own way out into the open, and a girl was born without the father knowing,
sentences.n: Se ipsum pondus expulit makes the child its own agent, with pondus, “weight”, still standing in for it. Ignaro patre is an ablative absolute with no participle, just noun and adjective — “the father being unaware”. Femina is the plain word for a female, and the poem uses it of Iphis again at IX.748, IX.790, IX.791 and in the inscription at IX.794.

sentences.t:
iussit ali mater puerum mentita: fidemque
res habuit, neque erat ficti nisi conscia nutrix.
sentences.l: the mother ordered it to be reared, having lied “a boy”: and the affair had credence, nor was anyone in on the pretence except the nurse.
sentences.i: the mother had it reared, passing it off as a boy — and the story was believed; nobody was in on the pretence but the nurse.
sentences.n: Mentita is the perfect participle of the deponent mentior and is active in sense, “having lied”, with puerum as the thing pretended. Ali is a present passive infinitive after iussit. Fidem res habuit is the idiom for a story being taken as true. Conscia, feminine, is the nurse who shares the knowledge.

sentences.t:
Vota pater solvit nomenque inponit avitum:
Iphis avus fuerat.
sentences.l: The father pays his vows and puts on the child an ancestral name: Iphis the grandfather had been.
sentences.i: The father pays his vows and gives the child a name from the family: the grandfather had been an Iphis.
sentences.n: Vota solvere is the fixed phrase for discharging a vow once the thing prayed for has happened, and the same verb comes back in the inscription at IX.794, with dona in place of vota: dona ... solvit. Nomen avitum is a name inherited from a grandfather, and the next clause explains which one.

sentences.t:
Gavisa est nomine mater,
quod commune foret nec quemquam falleret illo.
sentences.l: The mother rejoiced at the name, because it would be shared and she would deceive no one with it.
sentences.i: The mother was glad of the name, because it belonged to either sex and she would be deceiving nobody in using it.
sentences.n: Gavisa est is the semi-deponent gaudeo — passive in form in the perfect, active in sense. Commune here means common to both sexes: Iphis will fit a daughter as well as a son. Foret is an old form of esset, and both it and falleret are subjunctive because the reason given is hers, not the narrator's. Falleret is the same verb the goddess used at IX.697, mandata falle.

sentences.t:
Inde incepta pia mendacia fraude latebant:
cultus erat pueri, facies, quam sive puellae,
sive dares puero, fuerat formosus uterque.
sentences.l: From then on the lies lay hidden, the dutiful deceit once begun: the dress was a boy's, and the face was one which, whether you gave it to a girl or gave it to a boy, either would have been beautiful.
sentences.i: From then on the lies stayed hidden, once the dutiful fraud had been started: the clothes were a boy's, and the face was one you could have given to a girl or to a boy and either would have been beautiful.
sentences.n: Incepta pia fraude is an ablative absolute, “with the dutiful deception once begun”; pia recalls the pietas Ligdus appealed to at IX.679, now on the other side. Dares is the indefinite second person in the subjunctive — “whether you gave it”, of anyone at all — while the apodosis fuerat formosus is plain indicative, stating the outcome as fact where English can only say “would have been”. Uterque is masculine because it covers a boy and a girl together.

sentences.t:
Tertius interea decimo successerat annus,
cum pater, Iphi, tibi flavam despondet Ianthen,
sentences.l: Meanwhile a third year had followed on the tenth, when your father, Iphis, betroths golden-haired Ianthe to you,
sentences.i: Meanwhile the thirteenth year had come round, when your father, Iphis, betroths golden-haired Ianthe to you,
sentences.n: Tertius decimo successerat annus counts the year by addition — the third after the tenth. Iphi is a vocative: the poem turns aside from the narrative to speak to its character directly, and it does this again to Hymenaeus at IX.765 and to Iphis at IX.791; the vocatives at IX.744 and IX.762 are inside Iphis' own speech and are hers, not the poem's. Despondet is a present indicative after the pluperfect successerat, the historic present speeding the narrative up.

sentences.t:
inter Phaestiadas quae laudatissima formae
dote fuit virgo, Dictaeo nata Teleste.
sentences.l: a maiden who among the women of Phaestus was the most praised for the endowment of her beauty, born of Dictaean Telestes.
sentences.i: a girl who among the women of Phaestus was praised above all others for the gift of her looks, and whose father was Telestes of Dicte.
sentences.n: Formae dote is an ablative of respect, with dos, a dowry, used of what nature gave her rather than what her family did. Dictaeo nata Teleste is an ablative of origin — born from Telestes — with Dicte, the Cretan mountain, as his epithet. Phaestiadas, the women of Phaestus, is formed from the place named at IX.669.

sentences.t:
Par aetas, par forma fuit, primasque magistris
accepere artes, elementa aetatis, ab isdem.
sentences.l: Their age was equal, their beauty equal, and they received their first arts, the rudiments of their years, from the same teachers.
sentences.i: They were the same age and equally beautiful, and they had their first lessons, the rudiments proper to their years, from the same teachers.
sentences.n: Par ... par is repeated with no connective, which is how Latin makes a pair sound matched. Accepere is accepērunt again, the poetic third-person plural perfect flagged at IX.680. Isdem is the edition's own form of eisdem and is kept as printed.

sentences.t:
Hinc amor ambarum tetigit rude pectus et aequum
vulnus utrique dedit.
sentences.l: From this, love touched the untrained breast of them both and gave an equal wound to each.
sentences.i: Out of this, love touched both their inexperienced hearts and dealt each of them the same wound.
sentences.n: Ambarum is the feminine genitive plural of ambo — “of the two of them”, and the ending says both are girls, which the household does not know. Rude pectus, singular, is shared between them, and aequum vulnus insists the two loves are the same; the very next line takes the symmetry away.

sentences.l: But their confidence was unequal: Ianthe waits for the marriage and the time of the promised torch, and the one whom she thinks to be a man she believes will be her husband;
sentences.i: But their confidence was not equal: Ianthe waits for the wedding and the day of the promised torch, and the one she takes for a man she believes will be her husband;
sentences.n: Quam is feminine accusative — the poem's own grammar keeps Iphis a woman inside the sentence that reports Ianthe believing her a man. Virum is repeated in two senses: first “a man”, then “a husband”, which is the ordinary Latin word for it. Taeda, the pine torch carried in the wedding procession, stands for the wedding itself, and returns at IX.769.

sentences.t:
Iphis amat, qua posse frui desperat, et auget
hoc ipsum flammas, ardetque in virgine virgo;
sentences.l: Iphis loves one whom she despairs of being able to enjoy, and this very thing increases the flames, and a maiden burns for a maiden;
sentences.i: Iphis loves where she has no hope of enjoyment, that itself feeds the fire, and a girl is on fire for a girl;
sentences.n: Frui is a deponent taking the ablative, which is why the relative is qua and not quam; the literal keeps it active, “to enjoy”. Ardet in virgine has the ablative of the person one burns for. Virgine and virgo put the same noun at the two ends of the phrase, the word for an unmarried girl standing on both sides of the love.

sentences.t:
vixque tenens lacrimas “quis me manet exitus” inquit,
“cognita quam nulli, quam prodigiosa novaeque
cura tenet Veneris?
sentences.l: and scarcely holding back her tears she says, “What outcome awaits me, whom a passion holds that is known to no one, monstrous, a passion of a strange love?
sentences.i: and barely holding back her tears she says, “What end is waiting for me — held by a passion nobody has heard of, monstrous, a passion of a love with no name?
sentences.n: The relative quam is feminine accusative, referring to me: Iphis describes herself in the feminine throughout the speech. Cognita and prodigiosa are nominative and attach to cura, the passion, not to Iphis. Prodigiosus is what a prodigium is, a portent against the order of things, and it stands with the monstri of IX.667 and the monstra of IX.736 in sense, though not in root. Novae Veneris is “of a new Venus”, that is, of a kind of love not met before.

sentences.t:
Si di mihi parcere vellent,
parcere debuerant;
sentences.l: If the gods were willing to spare me, they ought to have spared me;
sentences.i: If the gods meant to spare me, spare me they should have;
sentences.n: Vellent is imperfect subjunctive in the protasis, so the willing is put as what is not the case. Debuerant is plain indicative, not subjunctive: with verbs of obligation Latin states the duty as a fact and leaves the unreality to the surrounding condition, where English says “ought to have”. Parcere is repeated across the two halves, and it takes the dative mihi.

sentences.t:
si non, et perdere vellent,
naturale malum saltem et de more dedissent.
sentences.l: if not, and they were willing to destroy me, they should at least have given me a natural affliction, one according to the usual way.
sentences.i: and if not — if they meant to ruin me — they should at least have given me some ordinary affliction, of the usual kind.
sentences.n: Dedissent is pluperfect subjunctive in the apodosis, the past unreal to match vellent. Naturale malum and de more make the same complaint twice: what she asks for is not relief but a trouble of the ordinary sort. De more is a prepositional phrase doing the work of an adjective beside naturale.

sentences.t:
Nec vaccam vaccae, nec equas amor urit equarum:
urit oves aries, sequitur sua femina cervum.
sentences.l: Neither does love of a cow burn a cow, nor love of mares burn mares: the ram burns the ewes, his own female follows the stag.
sentences.i: No cow is set alight by love of a cow, no mares by love of mares: the ram inflames the ewes, and the doe that is his follows the stag.
sentences.n: Vaccae and equarum are objective genitives with amor — the love that has a cow for its object. Amor urit stands once only, in the second clause, and has to be supplied for the first; then urit reappears with a new subject, aries. In sua femina cervum the reflexive sua agrees with femina and not with cervum — she is the stag's own female — and the clause reverses the arrangement, putting the female first and the male last, so the four clauses cover both directions.

sentences.t:
Sic et aves coeunt, interque animalia cuncta
femina femineo conrepta cupidine nulla est.
sentences.l: So too the birds pair, and among all animals there is no female seized by a female desire.
sentences.i: Birds pair off the same way, and among all animals there is not one female gripped by desire for a female.
sentences.n: Coeunt is the plain word for coming together to mate. Femineo cupidine is an ablative of means with conrepta, a perfect passive participle: the desire does the seizing. Nulla est carries the whole weight of the sentence to the end, and Iphis takes that same word up as her own in the next line.

sentences.t:
Vellem nulla forem! Ne non tamen omnia Crete
monstra ferat, taurum dilexit filia Solis,
sentences.l: I could wish I were none! Yet, so that Crete should not fail to bear every kind of monster, the daughter of the Sun loved a bull,
sentences.i: I wish I were no such creature! And yet, so Crete should lack no kind of monster, the daughter of the Sun loved a bull,
sentences.n: Nulla is feminine and picks up nulla est from the line before: she wishes she were the “none” the catalogue just claimed. Vellem is an imperfect subjunctive of unfulfilled wish, and forem is an old form of essem. Ne non ... ferat is a purpose clause with a double negative, so the sense is that Crete should be short of no monster; monstra is the same noun as the monstri of IX.667, there in the genitive. The Latin does not name the daughter of the Sun.

sentences.t:
femina nempe marem: meus est furiosior illo,
si verum profitemur, amor!
sentences.l: a female, to be sure, loved a male: my love is more frenzied than that one, if we declare the truth!
sentences.i: a female wanting a male, at least: mine is a madder love than that, if we are telling the truth!
sentences.n: The verb dilexit is not repeated; femina nempe marem is the bare pair of nouns with the loving understood from the line before. Nempe concedes the point that the earlier case was at least male and female. Illo is an ablative of comparison standing for that love, and amor is held back to the very end of the sentence. Profitemur is deponent and active in sense.

sentences.t:
Tamen illa secuta est
spem Veneris, tamen illa dolis et imagine vaccae
passa bovem est, et erat, qui deciperetur adulter!
sentences.l: Yet she followed a hope of love, yet she by tricks and the likeness of a cow submitted to the bull, and there was an adulterer to be deceived!
sentences.i: Yet she at least had a hope to follow, yet by trickery and a counterfeit cow she submitted to the bull, and there was an adulterer there to be taken in!
sentences.n: Secuta est and passa est are both deponent perfects, active in force. Tamen illa is repeated at the head of each clause, hammering the comparison. Qui deciperetur is a relative clause of characteristic with the subjunctive — “of the sort to be deceived” — and adulter is Iphis' word for the bull, thrown out at the end of the line: even that monstrous affair, she says, had a partner who could be fooled.

sentences.t:
Huc licet e toto sollertia confluat orbe,
ipse licet revolet ceratis Daedalus alis,
quid faciet?
sentences.l: Though all the world's ingenuity flow together here, though Daedalus himself fly back on his waxed wings, what will he do?
sentences.i: Let every cleverness in the world pour in here, let Daedalus himself come flying back on his waxed wings — what will he do?
sentences.n: Licet with the subjunctive (confluat, revolet) is concessive: “granted that”, “even if”. Sollertia is skill of the inventive kind, and it is what Daedalus stands for. Magnus prints e toto orbe; some editions print ex. Revolet has the re- of flying back, and Daedalus is named without any account of where he would be flying back from.

sentences.t:
Num me puerum de virgine doctis
artibus efficiet? num te mutabit, Ianthe?
sentences.l: Will he make me a boy out of a maiden by his learned arts? will he change you, Ianthe?
sentences.i: Will he turn me from a girl into a boy with his learned skills? will he change you, Ianthe?
sentences.n: Num introduces a question expecting the answer no, twice. De virgine is “out of a maiden”, the material one thing is made from. Doctis artibus is an ablative of means, and artes is the same word used of the girls' first lessons at IX.719. Ianthe is addressed by name here although she is not present, an aside inside the speech.

sentences.t:
Quin animum firmas, teque ipsa reconligis, Iphi,
consiliique inopes et stultos excutis ignes?
sentences.l: Why do you not steady your mind, and gather yourself up again, Iphis, and shake out these fires, destitute of counsel and foolish?
sentences.i: Why not brace your mind, pull yourself together, Iphis, and shake off these fires, senseless and stupid as they are?
sentences.n: Quin with the present indicative is an urging dressed as a question — “why not”, meaning “do it”. Iphis addresses herself by name and in the vocative, Iphi. Ipsa is feminine nominative, agreeing with the speaker. Consilii inopes is a genitive with inops, “destitute of judgement”. Reconligis is the edition's unassimilated spelling, kept as printed.

sentences.t:
Quid sis nata, vide, nisi te quoque decipis ipsa,
et pete quod fas est, et ama quod femina debes!
sentences.l: See what you were born as, unless you are deceiving yourself too, and seek what is right, and love what as a woman you ought!
sentences.i: See what you were born, unless you are taken in along with everyone else, and go after what is permitted, and love what a woman is bound to love!
sentences.n: Quid sis nata is an indirect question with the subjunctive, and nata is feminine: the ending is the answer to the question she is asking. Quoque is the adverb “also” — everyone else has been deceived by the pretence, and the warning is not to join them. Fas is what divine law allows, as against ius, what human law allows. Magnus prints ipsa, feminine nominative agreeing with the subject; some editions print ipsam, agreeing instead with te.

sentences.t:
Spes est, quae capiat, spes est, quae pascit amorem:
hanc tibi res adimit.
sentences.l: It is hope that catches love, it is hope that feeds love: this the fact takes away from you.
sentences.i: It is hope that catches love and hope that feeds it — and the fact of things takes that away from you.
sentences.n: Spes est quae ... is the cleft construction, putting hope in the predicate for emphasis and repeating it; amorem is the object of both relative clauses and is stated only once, at the end. Magnus prints capiat, subjunctive — a relative clause of characteristic, which English renders with a plain verb — beside the indicative pascit, which simply states; some editions print faciat and pascat, making both subjunctive and both characterising. Res is the state of affairs, and adimit takes the dative tibi of the person robbed.

sentences.t:
Non te custodia caro
arcet ab amplexu nec cauti cura mariti,
non patris asperitas, non se negat ipsa roganti:
sentences.l: No guard keeps you from a dear embrace, nor the vigilance of a wary husband, nor a father's harshness, nor does she herself refuse you when you ask:
sentences.i: No watchman keeps you from an embrace you long for, no careful husband's vigilance, no harsh father, and she herself does not say no when you ask:
sentences.n: Four obstacles are listed and each is denied — the guard, the husband, the father, the girl's own refusal — and non is repeated at the head of three of them. Roganti is a dative present participle with no noun: “to you asking”, supplied from te above. Se negat is the idiom for refusing oneself to a suitor.

sentences.t:
nec tamen est potienda tibi, nec, ut omnia fiant,
esse potes felix, ut dique hominesque laborent.
sentences.l: and yet she is not to be got by you, nor, though everything should come about, can you be happy, though gods and men should toil.
sentences.i: and still she cannot be yours, and even if everything else fell out right, even if gods and men worked at it, you could not be happy.
sentences.n: Potienda is a gerundive, feminine, agreeing with Ianthe: the thing that is or is not to be obtained. Potior takes the ablative and appears again as potitur in the last line of the tale, IX.797, where it is Iphis who does the obtaining. Both ut-clauses are concessive with the subjunctive, “even supposing that”.

sentences.t:
Nunc quoque votorum nulla est pars vana meorum,
dique mihi faciles, quidquid valuere, dederunt;
sentences.l: Now too no part of my prayers is empty, and the gods, obliging to me, have given whatever they had power to give;
sentences.i: As it is, not one part of my prayers has gone empty: the gods have been obliging and have given all they could;
sentences.n: Quoque here is the ordinary adverb “also”. Vana is the same word used of Telethusa's prayers at IX.682, where they did fail; Iphis says hers have not. Valuere is valuērunt, the poetic perfect flagged at IX.680, and quidquid is its object. Faciles of a god means easily won over.

sentences.t:
quodque ego, vult genitor, vult ipsa socerque futurus.
At non vult natura, potentior omnibus istis,
quae mihi sola nocet.
sentences.l: and what I want, my father wants, she herself wants, and my father-in-law to be. But nature does not want it, more powerful than all of those, she who alone harms me.
sentences.i: and what I want, my father wants, and she herself wants, and my father-in-law to be. Only nature does not want it — stronger than all of them, and the one thing that harms me.
sentences.n: The verb in quodque ego is left out and has to be supplied from the vult that follows. Vult stands twice in the line and is understood a third time with socerque futurus, so that four parties want it once the ego of quodque ego is counted; then it is denied at the head of the next line, at non vult, which is where the sentence turns. Istis is the demonstrative of the second person and is dismissive of the list just made. Quae and sola are feminine, agreeing with natura.

sentences.t:
Venit ecce optabile tempus,
luxque iugalis adest, et iam mea fiet Ianthe—
sentences.l: See, the longed-for time has come, and the wedding day is here, and now Ianthe will become mine—
sentences.i: Look, the time everyone wanted has come, the wedding day is here, and now Ianthe is to be mine—
sentences.n: Optabile is a verbal adjective, “to be wished for”, and by her own account two lines earlier, at IX.757, the wish is hers as much as anyone's. Lux iugalis is the day of the yoke, the wedding day. Magnus prints a dash: the thought breaks off at the height of it and the next clause takes it back.

sentences.t: nec mihi continget: mediis sitiemus in undis.
sentences.l: and yet it will not fall to my lot: we shall thirst in the midst of the waters.
sentences.i: and she will not be mine: we shall go thirsty in the middle of the water.
sentences.n: Contingit is impersonal and takes the dative of the person a thing falls to. Sitiemus is first-person plural: she puts Ianthe in the thirst with her. Mediis in undis is an ablative of place, and the image is of standing in water and getting none of it.

sentences.t:
Pronuba quid Iuno, quid ad haec, Hymenaee, venitis
sacra, quibus qui ducat abest, ubi nubimus ambae?”
sentences.l: Why, Juno of the bridal, why, Hymenaeus, do you come to these rites, at which the one who is to take the bride is absent, where we marry as brides, both of us?”
sentences.i: Why do you come to these rites, Juno of the bridal, why you, Hymenaeus — rites with no one to take the bride, where the two of us marry as brides?”
sentences.n: Pronuba is Juno's title as the matron who attends a bride. Latin keeps two verbs for marrying: ducere is what the man does, taking the woman home, and nubere is what the woman does; qui ducat is a relative of characteristic, “anyone to do the taking”, and nubimus puts both parties on the woman's side of the pair. Ambae is feminine nominative plural and is the last word of the speech.

sentences.t:
Pressit ab his vocem. Nec lenius altera virgo
aestuat, utque celer venias, Hymenaee, precatur.
sentences.l: After these words she pressed down her voice. Nor does the other maiden seethe any more gently, and she prays that you come swiftly, Hymenaeus.
sentences.i: With that she checked her voice. The other girl is no less feverish, and prays that you will come quickly, Hymenaeus.
sentences.n: Vocem premere is the same phrase used at IX.692 of the figure who holds his voice down, there a gesture of silence, here the end of a speech. Altera virgo of Ianthe implies Iphis is the first of the two. The prayer is reported in the second person, ut venias, so the narrative keeps addressing Hymenaeus as the speech did.

sentences.t:
Quod petit haec, Telethusa timens modo tempora differt,
nunc ficto languore moram trahit, omina saepe
visaque causatur.
sentences.l: What this one seeks, Telethusa in fear now puts off the times, now drags out delay with a feigned illness, often pleads omens and visions as her reason.
sentences.i: What the one girl is asking for, the frightened Telethusa keeps deferring — now putting the date back, now spinning out delay with a pretended illness, often giving out omens and visions as her reason.
sentences.n: Magnus prints Quod, neuter singular — the thing Ianthe is asking for — set at the head as what the delaying is aimed at; some editions print quae. Modo ... nunc is the pair for “now this, now that”. Ficto languore is an ablative of means, and ficti at IX.769 is the same participle used as a noun. Causari is deponent, active in sense: to plead a thing as a cause.

sentences.t:
Sed iam consumpserat omnem
materiam ficti, dilataque tempora taedae
institerant, unusque dies restabat.
sentences.l: But by now she had used up all the material of pretence, and the postponed time of the wedding torch had pressed close, and one day was left.
sentences.i: But by now she had used up all her material for pretending, the postponed date of the wedding had come pressing up, and one day was left.
sentences.n: Materiam ficti is the stuff a fiction is made of, ficti being the perfect participle used as a noun; the metaphor is of a supply running out. Instare is to stand over or press close, and the pluperfect institerant puts the pressing before the one remaining day. Taedae is again the wedding torch, as at IX.722.

sentences.t:
At illa
crinalem capiti vittam nataeque sibique
detrahit et passis aram complexa capillis
“Isi, Paraetonium Mareoticaque arva Pharonque
quae colis et septem digestum in cornua Nilum:
sentences.l: But she pulls the hair-band from her daughter's head and from her own, and, having embraced the altar with her hair let loose, “Isis, you who dwell in Paraetonium and the Mareotic fields and Pharos and the Nile parted into seven horns:
sentences.i: But she pulls the hair-band off her daughter's head and her own, and with her hair let down she takes hold of the altar: “Isis, you who dwell in Paraetonium and the Mareotic fields and Pharos and the Nile split into seven horns:
sentences.n: Natae, “her daughter's”, keeps Iphis feminine at the last moment before the change. Capiti, natae and sibi are all datives with detrahit — the head the band comes off, and the two people it is taken from. Passis capillis is an ablative absolute, “with the hair spread out”. Complexa is the deponent complector, active in sense. The Latin names Paraetonium, the Mareotic fields, Pharos and the Nile as the goddess's places and adds nothing about them; cornua, “horns”, is the ordinary word for the mouths of a river, and it is the same word used of the goddess's own headdress at IX.688–689.

sentences.t: fer, precor” inquit “opem nostroque medere timori!
sentences.l: bring, I pray,” she says, “help, and heal our fear!
sentences.i: bring us help, I pray,” she says, “and cure our fear!
sentences.n: Fer ... opem is prised apart — by precor inside the prayer and by inquit outside it — so that the verb and its object stand at opposite ends. Medere is the imperative of the deponent medeor and takes the dative timori — one heals a thing by treating it, so the fear itself is the patient. Nostro is the plural for the two of them.

sentences.t:
Te, dea, te quondam tuaque haec insignia vidi
cunctaque cognovi, sonitum comitantiaque aera
sistrorum, memorique animo tua iussa notavi.
sentences.l: You, goddess, you I once saw, and these emblems of yours, and I recognised them all, the sound and the accompanying bronze of the rattles, and I marked your commands in a remembering mind.
sentences.i: You, goddess, you I once saw, and these emblems of yours, and I knew them all — the noise and the bronze of the rattles that went with you — and I fixed your orders in a mind that has not forgotten.
sentences.n: Te is repeated at the head of the sentence for insistence, both times as the object of vidi. The rattles and the bronze are the sistra of IX.693, and the claim is that she is now naming what she saw then. Memori animo is an ablative of place or means with notavi, “marked in a mind that remembers”. Iussa is the neuter plural participle used as a noun, the things ordered at IX.697–699.

sentences.t:
Quod videt haec lucem, quod non ego punior, ecce
consilium munusque tuum est.
sentences.l: That this girl sees the light, that I am not punished — look, it is your counsel and your gift.
sentences.i: That this girl of mine is alive, that I go unpunished — that is your plan and your gift.
sentences.n: Two quod-clauses stand as the subject of est, and est stays singular although two predicate nouns follow it. Haec, feminine, is Iphis. Lucem videre is the idiom for being alive; punior is present passive, “I am being punished”, and what she is not being punished for is the disobedience at IX.706.

sentences.t:
Miserere duarum
auxilioque iuva!” Lacrimae sunt verba secutae.
sentences.l: Have pity on the two of us and help us with your aid!” Tears followed her words.
sentences.i: Pity the two of us, and come to our help!” Tears followed the words.
sentences.n: Misereor is deponent and takes the genitive of the person pitied; duarum is feminine, so the two she asks pity for are both women. Secutae sunt is again a deponent perfect, active in sense: the tears did the following.

sentences.t:
Visa dea est movisse suas (et moverat) aras,
et templi tremuere fores,
sentences.l: The goddess seemed to have moved her own altars (and she had moved them), and the doors of the temple trembled,
sentences.i: The goddess seemed to move her altars — and she had moved them — and the temple doors trembled,
sentences.n: Visa est with the perfect infinitive movisse leaves the seeming in the woman's mind and then the parenthesis et moverat corrects it as fact; the same hesitation was left standing at IX.688, aut stetit aut visa est, and here it is resolved. Tremuere is tremuērunt, the poetic perfect flagged at IX.680.

sentences.t:
imitataque lunam
cornua fulserunt, crepuitque sonabile sistrum.
sentences.l: and the horns imitating the moon flashed, and the sounding rattle clattered.
sentences.i: and the horns that copy the moon flashed, and the rattle gave its clatter.
sentences.n: Imitata is the perfect participle of the deponent imitor and is active in sense — the horns do the imitating. Both things named here are the ones described in the dream: the lunaria cornua of IX.688–689 and the sistra of IX.693. Sonabile is a verbal adjective, “able to sound”, so the rattle is called sounding before it sounds.

sentences.t:
Non secura quidem, fausto tamen omine laeta
mater abit templo:
sentences.l: Not free of care, indeed, but glad all the same at the favourable omen, the mother goes away from the temple:
sentences.i: Not easy in her mind, but glad all the same at the favourable sign, the mother leaves the temple:
sentences.n: Secura is se- plus cura, “apart from care”, and it answers the graves curas the goddess told her to put down at IX.697. Quidem ... tamen concedes and then corrects. Templo is a bare ablative of separation with abit, without a preposition.

sentences.t:
sequitur comes Iphis euntem,
quam solita est, maiore gradu, nec candor in ore
permanet, et vires augentur,
sentences.l: Iphis follows as companion the one going, with a longer stride than she was accustomed to, and the whiteness does not stay in her face, and her strength is increased,
sentences.i: Iphis follows her as she goes, keeping her company with a longer stride than usual, and the fairness does not stay in her face, and her strength grows,
sentences.n: Euntem is the accusative present participle of eo agreeing with the mother, who is not named again. Solita est is feminine, so the grammar still has Iphis as a woman in the same sentence in which the body begins to change. Maiore gradu is an ablative of manner. Candor is fair whiteness of complexion, prized in a girl, and it is the first thing to go.

sentences.t:
et acrior ipse est
vultus, et incomptis brevior mensura capillis,
plusque vigoris adest, habuit quam femina.
sentences.l: and the face itself is keener, and the measure of the uncombed hair is shorter, and more vigour is present than she had as a woman.
sentences.i: and the face itself is sharper, the uncombed hair shorter in its length, and there is more vigour than she had as a woman.
sentences.n: Acrior of a face is sharp-featured rather than soft. Incomptis capillis goes with mensura, the measure belonging to the uncombed hair — hair that was let down at IX.772. Femina here measures what Iphis had as a woman against what is arriving; the word is used of her twice more, at IX.791 and in the inscription at IX.794, each time for what she was.

sentences.t:
Nam quae
femina nuper eras, puer es.
sentences.l: For you who a moment ago were a woman, are a boy.
sentences.i: For you who were a girl a moment ago are a boy.
sentences.n: The poem turns aside to address Iphis directly, as it did at IX.715, and the change is announced by nothing but the two nouns and two tenses: eras against es, femina against puer. Quae, the relative, is still feminine because it looks back to what Iphis was.

sentences.t:
Date munera templis
nec timida gaudete fide!
sentences.l: Give gifts to the temples, and rejoice with no timid faith!
sentences.i: Give gifts to the temples, and rejoice — no timid faith about it!
sentences.n: Both imperatives are plural, so the poet is speaking to the mother and the child together. Timida fide is an ablative of manner with the negative attached to the adjective: the faith they are to rejoice with is not to be the frightened kind. Timida answers the timori, the fear, that the mother asked to have healed at IX.775.

sentences.t:
Dant munera templis,
addunt et titulum; titulus breve carmen habebat:
sentences.l: They give gifts to the temples, and they add an inscription as well; the inscription had a short verse:
sentences.i: They do give gifts to the temples, and add an inscription too; the inscription carried a short verse:
sentences.n: Dant munera templis repeats the poet's own command from the line before with nothing changed but the mood, the indicative answering the imperative: the command is answered by the deed. Titulus is the inscribed label on a dedication, and carmen here is a line of verse rather than a song.

sentences.t: DONA PUER SOLVIT QUAE FEMINA VOVERAT IPHIS
sentences.l: IPHIS AS A BOY PAID THE GIFTS WHICH AS A WOMAN HE HAD VOWED
sentences.i: IPHIS PAID AS A BOY WHAT HE HAD VOWED AS A GIRL
sentences.n: The edition prints the inscription in capitals and gives it no closing stop. It is a single dactylic hexameter, and it is built out of two matched pairs: puer against femina, solvit against voverat, with the subject Iphis held back to the last word so that the one name covers both. Vota solvere was the father's act at IX.708; the same verb is now the child's, with dona for vota. The Latin needs no pronoun anywhere — the one subject Iphis carries both puer and femina — where English has to choose one. Puer and femina are both in apposition to Iphis, each naming what the same person was at a different time.

sentences.t:
Postera lux radiis latum patefecerat orbem,
cum Venus et Iuno sociosque Hymenaeus ad ignes
conveniunt,
sentences.l: The next day's light had thrown open the broad world with its rays, when Venus and Juno and Hymenaeus come together to the shared fires,
sentences.i: The next day's light had opened up the wide world with its rays, when Venus and Juno and Hymenaeus come together at the shared fires,
sentences.n: Patefecerat is pluperfect and conveniunt is a historic present, the alternation that keeps speeding the narrative up and slowing it down. Socios ignes are the fires the wedding shares, and two of the three are the ones Iphis called on in her complaint at IX.762 — Juno the bridal matron and Hymenaeus — with Venus added here and the complaint answered.

sentences.t: potiturque sua puer Iphis Ianthe.
sentences.l: and the boy Iphis takes possession of his own Ianthe.
sentences.i: and Iphis, now a boy, has his own Ianthe.
sentences.n: Potitur is a deponent and active in sense, and it takes the ablative, which is why Ianthe is not accusative; it answers the gerundive potienda of IX.753, where Iphis said Ianthe was not to be had. Sua is the reflexive possessive, “his own”, and puer stands beside the name to say which Iphis this now is.
